explanation_en: A very common transition phrase used in journalism, essays, and formal speech to introduce a highly probable conclusion based on current evidence. It is a more sophisticated alternative to 'parece que' or 'es probable que' and helps structure advanced arguments smoothly.

examples.en_text: All signs point to it raining this weekend, so we'd better cancel the excursion.
examples.target_text: Todo indica que va a llover este fin de semana, así que mejor cancelamos la excursión.

examples.en_text: Everything indicates that the company is going to hire more staff next month.
examples.target_text: Todo indica que la empresa va a contratar a más personal el próximo mes.

examples.en_text: All signs point to the suspect fleeing the country before the police arrived.
examples.target_text: Todo indica que el sospechoso huyó del país antes de que llegara la policía.

examples.en_text: Everything indicates that electric cars will be the only option in a few years.
examples.target_text: Todo indica que los coches eléctricos serán la única opción en unos años.

examples.en_text: The patient feels much better and all signs point to them being discharged tomorrow.
examples.target_text: El paciente se siente mucho mejor y todo indica que le darán el alta mañana.

examples.en_text: They haven't spoken to each other for days; everything indicates that they have ended their relationship.
examples.target_text: No se hablan desde hace días; todo indica que han terminado su relación.

explanation_en: Derived from the idiom 'la otra cara de la moneda' (the other side of the coin), 'la otra cara de [algo]' is used to describe the opposite, often negative or lesser-known, aspect of a situation. It is a staple of journalistic and analytical Spanish to introduce contrast.

examples.en_text: Tourism brings money, but the other side of the coin is the increase in prices for locals.
examples.target_text: El turismo trae dinero, pero la otra cara es el aumento de los precios para los locales.

examples.en_text: Working from home is comfortable, but the other side of the coin is the lack of social contact.
examples.target_text: Trabajar desde casa es cómodo, pero la otra cara de la moneda es la falta de contacto social.

examples.en_text: Winning the award was incredible, but then we learned the other side of success: the constant pressure.
examples.target_text: Ganar el premio fue increíble, pero luego conocimos la otra cara del éxito: la presión constante.

examples.en_text: Social networks connect us, but the other side of the coin is that they sometimes isolate us from reality.
examples.target_text: Las redes sociales nos conectan, pero la otra cara es que a veces nos aíslan de la realidad.

examples.en_text: Living in a big city is exciting, although the other side of the coin is the daily stress.
examples.target_text: Vivir en una gran ciudad es emocionante, aunque la otra cara es el estrés diario.

examples.en_text: Accepting the new position means a better salary, but the other side of the coin is that I will have less free time.
examples.target_text: Aceptar el nuevo puesto significa un mejor sueldo, pero la otra cara es que tendré menos tiempo libre.

explanation_en: This is a standard journalistic collocation used to report rising numbers, especially casualties, costs, or statistics. The verb 'elevar' (to raise/elevate) is preferred over 'subir' in news reporting to maintain a formal register. Pay attention to the prepositional structure: 'elevar [algo] a [número]'.

examples.en_text: The government's latest report has raised the number of people affected by the storm to more than ten thousand.
examples.target_text: El último informe del gobierno ha elevado la cifra de damnificados por la tormenta a más de diez mil personas.

examples.en_text: The success of the new car model raises the company's sales figures to a record level.
examples.target_text: El éxito del nuevo modelo de coche eleva la cifra de ventas de la empresa a un nivel récord.

examples.en_text: The arrival of tourists this summer will raise the number of visitors to the island to one million.
examples.target_text: La llegada de turistas este verano elevará la cifra de visitantes a la isla a un millón.

examples.en_text: The new flu cases raise the number of sick people in the city to more than a thousand.
examples.target_text: Los nuevos casos de gripe elevan la cifra de enfermos en la ciudad a más de mil.

examples.en_text: The opening of the new factory has raised the number of jobs created in the region to two thousand.
examples.target_text: La apertura de la nueva fábrica ha elevado la cifra de empleos creados en la región a dos mil.

examples.en_text: This year's graduation raises the number of professionals trained at the university to ten thousand.
examples.target_text: La graduación de este año eleva la cifra de profesionales formados en la universidad a diez mil.

explanation_en: The verb 'ceder' literally means to yield or give in, but in weather, fire, or health contexts, it means to subside, weaken, or lose intensity. It is a highly natural way to describe a storm passing, a fever breaking, or a fire being contained. It belongs to a mid-to-high register (B2/C1) and is very common in news reports.

examples.en_text: The storm is finally beginning to subside and the sky is clearing up.
examples.target_text: La tormenta por fin comienza a ceder y el cielo se está aclarando.

examples.en_text: Take this syrup; you'll see how the headache begins to subside in a few minutes.
examples.target_text: Tómate este jarabe; verás cómo el dolor de cabeza comienza a ceder en unos minutos.

examples.en_text: After he apologized, the tension in the office began to ease.
examples.target_text: Después de disculparse, la tensión en la oficina comenzó a ceder.

examples.en_text: The bridge is very old and the wood is already beginning to give way under the weight of the cars.
examples.target_text: El puente es muy viejo y la madera ya comienza a ceder bajo el peso de los coches.

examples.en_text: With the new economic measures, the pressure on prices is beginning to ease.
examples.target_text: Con las nuevas medidas económicas, la presión sobre los precios comienza a ceder.

examples.en_text: At first they didn't want to negotiate, but now their rigid stance is beginning to yield.
examples.target_text: Al principio no querían negociar, pero ahora su postura rígida comienza a ceder.

explanation_en: The construction 'no estar para + [noun/infinitivo]' is an idiomatic way to say 'to not be in the mood for' or 'to not be in a position to do' something. In this context, it expresses that the current critical situation does not allow for mistakes or improvisation. It is highly common in both everyday spoken Spanish and political commentary.

examples.en_text: We are in no position to waste time; the train leaves in ten minutes.
examples.target_text: No estamos para perder el tiempo; el tren sale en diez minutos.

examples.en_text: Today I'm in no mood for jokes; I've had a very difficult day at work.
examples.target_text: Hoy no estoy para bromas, he tenido un día muy difícil en el trabajo.

examples.en_text: With this crisis, we are in no position to spend money on unnecessary things.
examples.target_text: Con esta crisis, no estamos para gastar dinero en cosas innecesarias.

examples.en_text: My grandparents are no longer in a position to make such long trips.
examples.target_text: Mis abuelos ya no están para hacer viajes tan largos.

examples.en_text: You are in no position to demand much after what you did.
examples.target_text: No estás para exigir mucho después de lo que hiciste.

examples.en_text: The company is in no position to take on more risks this year.
examples.target_text: La empresa no está para asumir más riesgos este año.

explanation_en: 'Cobrar' usually means to charge or collect money, but in the context of disasters, accidents, or diseases, 'cobrar vidas' is a fixed idiomatic collocation meaning 'to claim lives'. It is a standard journalistic expression that advanced learners should adopt instead of literal translations like 'reclamar vidas'.

examples.en_text: Last week's earthquake claimed lives in several southern cities.
examples.target_text: El terremoto de la semana pasada cobró vidas en varias ciudades del sur.

examples.en_text: Unfortunately, the terrible disease claimed many lives before a cure was found.
examples.target_text: Lamentablemente, la terrible enfermedad cobró muchas vidas antes de que se encontrara una cura.

examples.en_text: That dangerous intersection has already claimed several lives this year.
examples.target_text: Ese peligroso cruce de calles ya ha cobrado varias vidas este año.

examples.en_text: The armed conflict claimed innocent lives for more than a decade.
examples.target_text: El conflicto armado cobró vidas inocentes durante más de una década.

examples.en_text: The severe winter storm claimed lives due to the extreme temperatures.
examples.target_text: La fuerte tormenta invernal cobró vidas debido a las temperaturas extremas.

examples.en_text: The fire at the shopping mall did not claim lives, but it caused serious property damage.
examples.target_text: El incendio en el centro comercial no cobró vidas, pero causó graves daños materiales.

explanation_en: This is the standard Spanish idiom for 'to earn a living' or 'to make a living'. While 'ganar' means to win or earn, adding the reflexive pronoun ('ganarse') shifts the meaning specifically to earning one's livelihood through work. It is highly common across all registers of Spanish.

examples.en_text: He earns a living writing mystery novels.
examples.target_text: Él se gana la vida escribiendo novelas de misterio.

examples.en_text: It's not easy to earn a living as an independent artist these days.
examples.target_text: No es fácil ganarse la vida como artista independiente en estos días.

examples.en_text: How do you earn a living in a city as expensive as this one?
examples.target_text: ¿Cómo te ganas la vida en una ciudad tan cara como esta?

examples.en_text: My grandparents earned a living working in the fields.
examples.target_text: Mis abuelos se ganaban la vida trabajando en el campo.

examples.en_text: I would like to earn a living doing something I am truly passionate about.
examples.target_text: Me gustaría ganarme la vida haciendo algo que realmente me apasione.

examples.en_text: Currently, she is earning a living as a freelance translator.
examples.target_text: Actualmente, ella se está ganando la vida como traductora autónoma.

explanation_en: This expression means 'to turn to ashes' or 'to reduce to ashes', indicating complete destruction by fire. It can be used literally, as in a building burning down, or metaphorically to describe hopes, dreams, or plans being utterly ruined. It is a powerful, highly descriptive collocation.

examples.en_text: The forest fire turned thousands of hectares of forest into ashes in just a few hours.
examples.target_text: El incendio forestal convirtió en cenizas miles de hectáreas de bosque en pocas horas.

examples.en_text: All our plans to travel this year turned to ashes due to the economic crisis.
examples.target_text: Todos nuestros planes de viajar este año se convirtieron en cenizas debido a la crisis económica.

examples.en_text: The fire has turned the old documents we kept in the attic into ashes.
examples.target_text: El fuego ha convertido en cenizas los viejos documentos que guardábamos en el desván.

examples.en_text: If we don't take care of our friendship, everything we built will turn to ashes.
examples.target_text: Si no cuidamos nuestra amistad, todo lo que construimos se convertirá en cenizas.

examples.en_text: I decided to burn the photos of my past and turn them into ashes to start over.
examples.target_text: Decidí quemar las fotos de mi pasado y convertirlas en cenizas para empezar de nuevo.

examples.en_text: In a matter of minutes, the beautiful wooden cabin turned to ashes.
examples.target_text: En cuestión de minutos, la hermosa cabaña de madera se convirtió en cenizas.

explanation_en: The verb 'cernerse' (literally to hover or hang over) is used metaphorically with the preposition 'sobre' to describe a threat, danger, or negative feeling looming over a place or person. It is a sophisticated C1-level verb that adds dramatic tension and is highly favored in journalism and literature.

examples.en_text: A dark storm looms over the coast this afternoon.
examples.target_text: Una tormenta oscura se cierne sobre la costa esta tarde.

examples.en_text: The shadow of doubt looms over the election results.
examples.target_text: La sombra de la duda se cierne sobre el resultado de las elecciones.

examples.en_text: A serious financial crisis looms over the small family business.
examples.target_text: Una grave crisis financiera se cierne sobre el pequeño negocio familiar.

examples.en_text: New threats of layoffs loom over the factory workers.
examples.target_text: Nuevas amenazas de despido se ciernen sobre los trabajadores de la fábrica.

examples.en_text: The mystery of their disappearance still looms over the town.
examples.target_text: El misterio de su desaparición aún se cierne sobre el pueblo.

examples.en_text: The final physics exam looms over us and everyone is nervous.
examples.target_text: El examen final de física se cierne sobre nosotros y todos están nerviosos.

explanation_en: An 'elucubración' is a complex, often far-fetched speculation, theory, or conjecture. Saying 'no hablar de elucubraciones' means dealing with hard, physical facts rather than wild theories. It is a sophisticated, high-level vocabulary word (C1) used in intellectual debates and analytical journalism.

examples.en_text: Let's put aside the speculations and focus on the real data we have.
examples.target_text: Dejemos a un lado las elucubraciones y concentrémonos en los datos reales que tenemos.

examples.en_text: Everything being said about his resignation is just speculation by the press.
examples.target_text: Todo lo que se dice sobre su renuncia son solo elucubraciones de la prensa.

examples.en_text: I don't want to waste time with speculations; I prefer to ask him directly what happened.
examples.target_text: No quiero perder el tiempo con elucubraciones; prefiero preguntarle directamente qué pasó.

examples.en_text: Without scientific proof, your theories are nothing more than simple speculations.
examples.target_text: Sin pruebas científicas, tus teorías no son más que simples elucubraciones.

examples.en_text: I spent the whole night lost in my own speculations and couldn't sleep at all.
examples.target_text: Pasé toda la noche perdido en mis propias elucubraciones y no pude dormir nada.

examples.en_text: The police cannot base their investigation on mere speculations from the neighbors.
examples.target_text: La policía no puede basar su investigación en meras elucubraciones de los vecinos.

explanation_en: 'Dejar huella' (or 'dejar huellas') means to leave a footprint, mark, or lasting impression. It can refer to physical traces left behind or, more commonly, to a profound emotional or historical impact. It is a very common, versatile idiom used in both casual and formal contexts.

examples.en_text: A good teacher doesn't just teach the subject, but leaves a mark on their students' lives.
examples.target_text: Un buen profesor no solo enseña la materia, sino que deja huella en la vida de sus alumnos.

examples.en_text: If you walk barefoot on the wet sand, you leave footprints that the sea will soon wash away.
examples.target_text: Si caminas descalzo por la arena mojada, dejas huellas que el mar borrará pronto.

examples.en_text: First love is a beautiful experience that always leaves its mark on our hearts.
examples.target_text: El primer amor es una experiencia hermosa que siempre deja huella en nuestro corazón.

examples.en_text: Be careful when touching the clean window, because your hand leaves very easy-to-see fingerprints.
examples.target_text: Ten cuidado al tocar la ventana limpia, porque tu mano deja huellas muy fáciles de ver.

examples.en_text: That movie about the war is excellent and leaves a deep mark on anyone who watches it.
examples.target_text: Esa película sobre la guerra es excelente y deja una huella profunda en cualquiera que la vea.

examples.en_text: The passage of time is inevitable and leaves visible marks on the walls of this old castle.
examples.target_text: El paso del tiempo es inevitable y deja huellas visibles en las paredes de este viejo castillo.

explanation_en: While 'atravesar' literally means 'to cross' or 'to go through' physically, in figurative contexts it means to experience or undergo a difficult situation or crisis. It is highly common in news, business, and formal speech when discussing economic downturns, emotional states, or transitional phases. Note that it is transitive and does not require a preposition when meaning 'to experience' (e.g., 'atravesar una crisis').

examples.en_text: Many local businesses are going through an economic crisis due to the lack of tourism.
examples.target_text: Muchas empresas locales atraviesan una crisis económica debido a la falta de turismo.

examples.en_text: Currently, we are going through a time of constant changes at work.
examples.target_text: Actualmente atravesamos una época de cambios constantes en el trabajo.

examples.en_text: Several countries in the region are going through a period of great political instability.
examples.target_text: Varios países de la región atraviesan un período de gran inestabilidad política.

examples.en_text: Our family is going through a delicate situation, but we are staying united.
examples.target_text: Nuestra familia atraviesa una situación delicada, pero nos mantenemos unidos.

examples.en_text: Teenagers often go through stages of rebellion and confusion.
examples.target_text: Los adolescentes a menudo atraviesan etapas de rebeldía y confusión.

examples.en_text: The farmers in the area are going through a very tough situation due to the lack of rain.
examples.target_text: Los agricultores de la zona atraviesan una situación muy dura por la falta de lluvias.
